questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The blast radius of one identity provider
questions.learningObjective: Explain the exposure created when every account depends on one identity provider
questions.stem: The dispatch office signs every crew member in to the scheduling system through a single external identity provider. If that provider is compromised, what reaches the railway's own systems?

options.text: Every account federated through it, because one trust relationship carries access for all of them
Nothing, because the provider holds no credentials of its own and only passes on assertions
options.misconception: believes assertion passing prevents account takeover

options.text: Only the accounts that were used on the day of the compromise, since sessions expire each shift
options.misconception: believes session lifetime limits the blast radius

options.text: Only the roster data, because the provider stores no permissions for railway systems
options.misconception: believes the provider holds no permissions

questions.explanation: One provider acting as the federation point for every crew account means a compromise there is equivalent to a compromise of all those accounts. Trust is established once, so the failure is shared by everything downstream of it.
questions.hint: Ask how many accounts share the same trust.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A service principal and a platform identity are not the same
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an application held principal from a platform issued identity
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log records a nightly job that pulls departure boards. It authenticates with a service principal stored in the application repository, and the cloud platform also grants it a managed role. Which is the platform identity?

options.text: The service principal, because both names describe a non-human caller and the platform records it too
options.misconception: treats the two names as interchangeable

options.text: The managed role the platform creates and controls, not the application held principal
The service principal, because it is the only credential that can be listed in the repository
options.misconception: identifies the principal by where it is stored

options.text: Neither, because the platform role is only a label for the same service principal
options.misconception: assumes a platform role is a nickname for a principal

questions.explanation: A platform identity is created and governed by the platform, with its own lifecycle, while a service principal is an application held credential that the platform merely records. Conflating them hides who can rotate, delete and audit the credential.
questions.hint: Ask who created and controls the credential.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Federation trust runs one way
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequences of a one-way federation for the railway
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log notes that the signalling contractor's platform can issue tickets to the railway's access system, but the railway's platform cannot issue tickets back. Explain what this one-way trust means for the railway.

answer.exemplar: The relationship is a unilateral federation in which the contractor's identity provider is configured as a trusted issuer in the railway's access system, while the railway's provider is not listed as a trusted issuer for the contractor. Every contractor user can therefore sign in to railway resources, but no railway user can sign in to contractor resources, so the railway gains an external user population it must govern without gaining any reciprocal visibility of contractor-side access. The consequence is asymmetric risk: the railway carries the full burden of assessing and revoking contractor identities, while the contractor's users can reach railway systems through a path the railway cannot observe from the other end, so the railway must also decide what happens to those sessions when the relationship ends.

questions.explanation: The contractor's provider is a trusted issuer for the railway and the reverse does not hold, so the railway gains external access it must govern alone. Revocation, monitoring and exit planning all sit with the railway.
questions.hint: Ask who can issue tickets into which system.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a private endpoint does not do for authorisation
questions.learningObjective: Separate the network effect of a private endpoint from authorisation

stimulus.body: At 03:12 the dispatcher recorded that the depot telemetry service began timing out. The platform team attached a private endpoint to the service so that its traffic to the data store no longer crosses the public network. The following day the store's audit log showed the service account writing to tables it had never written to before, and the account still held the same role it held the week before.

questions.stem: According to the dispatcher log above, what does the private endpoint change?

options.text: It removes the public network path, so the unexpected writes must have come from the depot itself
options.misconception: assumes removing a path removes the cause

options.text: It grants the service a trusted network location, so the new writes are a result of the endpoint
options.misconception: treats network location as a source of authority

options.text: It changes only the network path, so the writes are explained by the unchanged role rather than the endpoint
It removes the need for the role entirely, so the unexpected writes must come from another account
options.misconception: assumes the endpoint removes the need for a role

questions.explanation: A private endpoint changes where traffic travels, not what a caller may do. The account kept the same role, so the writes follow from permissions that were already granted, and the endpoint simply gave them a quieter route.
questions.hint: Ask what the endpoint changed and what it left.

options.misconception: invents confidentiality for a signed link and denies risk

options.text: A long-lived key gives short-lived access, while a signed link gives the same thing with more paperwork
options.misconception: reverses which mechanism is short-lived

options.text: A signed link removes all risk, while a long-lived key is safe because the display service is internal
options.misconception: believes internal services remove key risk

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Rewrapping and re-encrypting are different jobs
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a rewrap changes and what it leaves untouched
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log records a key rotation that rewrapped 240 stored manifests under a new key while leaving the ciphertext untouched. What does rewrapping actually change?

options.text: It changes the key material protecting each ciphertext, without decrypting and re-encrypting the payload
It decrypts every manifest and encrypts it again under the new key, so the stored bytes change
options.misconception: confuses rewrapping with re-encrypting the payload

options.text: It replaces the stored manifests with fresh copies generated from the source database
options.misconception: believes rewrapping regenerates the stored records

options.text: It rotates the signing certificate used by the manifest feed, leaving the encryption key untouched
options.misconception: confuses key rotation with certificate rotation

questions.explanation: Rewrapping changes only the key material around an existing ciphertext, which is fast and does not expose the payload. Re-encrypting would decrypt and encrypt the contents again, which is slower and risks the data if the process fails partway.
questions.hint: Ask whether the stored bytes change.

options.text: The replacement was applied correctly, because the file on disk now holds the new value
options.misconception: treats a file edit as a runtime change

options.text: The new value was only written, not loaded, because the running process still holds the old secret
The new key was rejected by the service, so the operator should request a different one from the issuer
options.misconception: jumps to key rejection without evidence

options.text: The configuration file is not the authoritative copy, so the change will never reach the service
options.misconception: assumes the file cannot be authoritative

questions.explanation: Writing a new secret to a file changes what is stored, not what a running process holds. Until the service reloads or restarts, requests keep using the previous value, so the rotation is incomplete on the wire.
questions.hint: Ask what the running process is holding.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A service principal and a platform identity are not the same
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a principal and a platform identity differ in lifecycle and ownership
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log names two credentials used by the same depot application: a service principal held in the application's own repository, and a platform identity created by the cloud platform. Explain how they differ and why the distinction matters.

answer.exemplar: A service principal is a credential the application owns and stores, commonly as an identifier and secret held in a repository or vault, and the platform records the corresponding object so that policies and sign-in logs refer to it. A platform identity is created and governed by the platform itself, with the platform assigning, rotating and expiring it and no secret ever handled by the application. The distinction matters because the two have different lifecycles and different owners. A service principal can be copied into another system, posted to a log or left in a configuration file, and it does not expire on its own. A platform identity can be disabled centrally, can be issued with a short life, and can have its own access policy attached, so it gives the railway a way to bound a workload's access that a stored secret cannot.

questions.explanation: The service principal is application held and copyable, while the platform identity is created, rotated and disabled by the platform. The difference decides how access is bounded and how a leak is contained.
questions.hint: Ask who can rotate and revoke each one.

questions.topic: A permission boundary narrowing a role
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a boundary applied in one environment only

stimulus.body: The dispatcher noted that the platform engineer attached a permission boundary to the analyst role used for train movement planning. The engineer recorded that the boundary was applied to the production copy of the role and not to the one used in the test environment.

questions.stem: Reading the dispatcher log above, which reading is correct?

options.text: The boundary has no effect until it is attached to every copy of the role in every environment
options.misconception: believes a boundary must be applied everywhere at once

options.text: The boundary should have been attached to the test role first, since production must mirror the test estate
options.misconception: prioritises test estate parity over production safety

options.text: The boundary narrows the production role to 6 actions, and the test copy remains unbounded
The boundary has removed the two excluded actions from the role definition itself
options.misconception: believes a boundary edits the role definition

questions.explanation: A permission boundary caps the actions a role can take in the scope where it is attached. Here it caps production to 6 actions while the test copy of the role keeps all 14, so the two environments now differ.
questions.hint: Ask where the boundary was attached and what it caps.

questions.stem: The dispatcher's log shows the display service fetching the timetable feed with a key that was issued in March and has no expiry recorded. A second entry shows the same service using a signed link that expires after four hours. What does the pair of entries show?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Replacing a secret in a configuration file
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a logged secret replacement must be followed by
questions.stem: A dispatcher service reads its data-store key from a configuration file, and the file was updated during the last maintenance window. Explain what the operator must do for the change to take effect and what the log should record.

answer.exemplar: The operator has to establish that the running process picked up the new value, because a service normally reads its configuration once at start and keeps the value in memory. Writing the file changes what is stored on disk, and the old key may still be in use until the service is restarted or explicitly told to reload, so the log should record the moment of the change, the restart or reload that consumed it, and the verification that the service authenticated with the new value. If the new key is rejected, the service may fall back to the old one or fail closed, and only the log tells the operator which happened, so a rotation cannot be closed out on the strength of the file edit alone.

questions.explanation: A file edit is not a runtime change, because the process usually read its configuration at start. The log needs the reload or restart, the time it happened and confirmation that the new value was actually used.
questions.hint: Ask when the process last read the file.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A signed link against a long-lived read key
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a non-expiring key is a standing exposure
questions.stem: The depot timetable display fetches its feed with a long-lived read key that has no expiry date. Explain why this is a standing exposure and what the railway could use instead.

answer.exemplar: A key with no expiry is a standing credential, so it stays usable for as long as the service presents it and until somebody notices and revokes it. Nothing about the credential itself forces that notice, and the ways it usually leaks are mundane: it sits in a configuration file, it appears in a support log, or it is copied into a test harness that is forgotten. The railway can reduce the exposure by replacing the key with a signed link, which is bound to a single request and carries a short expiry, so a copy of it is worthless within hours. The costs of that change are that the feed has to accept signed requests, the service needs a signing key or certificate of its own, and the clocks across the fleet have to be synchronised so that signatures are not rejected as being from the future.

questions.explanation: A key with no expiry is usable until somebody revokes it, so a copy stays useful for an unbounded time. A signed link expires in hours, which bounds the damage a copy can do.
questions.hint: Ask how long a copied credential stays useful.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Federation trust runs one way
questions.learningObjective: Explain the governance a one-way federation leaves with the railway
questions.stem: The railway federates with a signalling contractor so contractor engineers can reach the timetable planning tools. The contractor cannot reach the railway's other systems. Explain the security consequence of this arrangement.

answer.exemplar: The relationship is deliberately one-way, which means the railway accepts identities issued by the contractor without the contractor accepting any in return. That gives the railway an external population it must govern in full: it decides which contractor roles map to which railway permissions, it must be able to revoke those mappings, and it must be able to tell its own auditors who signed in and from where. The contractor, meanwhile, has no reciprocal view, so the railway cannot rely on the contractor to report suspicious activity, and the contractor cannot be given a railway-wide token that would let its own engineers wander into signalling systems it never intended to expose. Every additional contractor system that is federated in widens this one-way trust, so the number of federated systems is itself a quantity the railway should track and review, and the relationship needs an end condition that removes the trust rather than simply lapsing.

questions.explanation: A one-way trust means the railway governs contractor identities alone and cannot rely on the other side for visibility or revocation. Each additional federated system widens that single-sided responsibility.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the revocation power.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A service principal and a platform identity are not the same
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a migration to a platform identity changes and leaves
questions.stem: The depot application currently stores a service principal in its own repository. The platform team proposes migrating it to a platform identity. Explain what the migration would change and what it would not.

answer.exemplar: The migration would move the credential's lifecycle from the application to the platform. Today the application generates, stores, rotates and presents the secret, which means the secret exists wherever the application puts it and is only ever rotated when somebody remembers. With a platform identity the platform issues the credential, expires it on a fixed schedule and can disable it centrally in an emergency, so the railway gains a revocation lever it does not have today and the workload gains a bounded exposure window instead of a standing secret. What the migration would not change is the workload's behaviour: the same role would still define which actions it can take, the same data would be read and written, and the same network paths would be used. The team should be clear that a platform identity is a governance improvement rather than a permission reduction, and that any tightening of access has to be designed separately.

questions.explanation: The migration moves issuance, expiry and revocation to the platform and leaves the workload's behaviour and role untouched. It is a governance gain, not an automatic reduction in access.
questions.hint: Ask what the role still says after the move.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Replacing a secret in a configuration file
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk of an un-reloaded secret replacement
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log shows a depot service reading its data-store credential from a mounted configuration file, and the file was edited during a maintenance window without the service being restarted. Explain the risk this leaves and what should have been done.

answer.exemplar: The edit changed what was stored, not what the running process held, so the service kept presenting the previous credential and the old value remained live on the wire for the rest of the shift. That matters because a rotation is only real when the retired value stops being accepted, and an unnoticed continuation leaves a credential in use that the operator believes has been replaced, which is precisely the state in which a leak of the old value continues to work after the paperwork says it was retired. The correct handling is to edit the file and then force the service to reload or restart inside the same window, confirm from the service's own logs that the new value was used on the following request, revoke the old credential so it cannot be used even by a service that has not restarted, and record the times of the edit, the reload and the revocation in the log so that the rotation can be audited later.

questions.explanation: A file edit without a reload leaves the old credential live, so the rotation is only real once the service demonstrably uses the new value and the old one is revoked and recorded.
questions.hint: Ask what the running service is still presenting.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A signed link against a long-lived read key
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a signed link reduces exposure and what it costs
questions.stem: The railway wants to stop storing a long-lived read key for the timetable feed. Explain why a signed link reduces the exposure and what the railway must change to make it work.

answer.exemplar: A long-lived key is a standing secret that works until somebody revokes it, and the usual leaks are ordinary rather than exotic: a value in a configuration file, a line in a support log, a copy pasted into a test harness. Because nothing about the key expires, the railway has no natural signal that tells it when to worry, so the exposure is bounded only by revocation discipline. A signed link is bound to a request and carries a short expiry, so a copy of it stops working within hours and the value of stealing it falls sharply. Making the change requires the feed's owner to accept and validate signatures, the service to hold a signing key or certificate, and the clocks across the service fleet to be synchronised, because a skewed clock produces rejected signatures that look like outages. The railway should treat the retirement of the old key as part of the same change rather than leaving both in service.

questions.explanation: A signed link bounds how long a leak is worth, where a standing key stays usable until revoked. The switch needs feed support for signatures, a signing credential in the service and reliable clocks.
questions.hint: Ask what expires in each case.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Federation trust runs one way
questions.learningObjective: Set out the duties a one-way federation leaves with the railway
questions.stem: The railway federates with two contractor platforms so their engineers can use the timetable planning tools. Explain what the railway takes on and what it cannot delegate.

answer.exemplar: Taking on federation means taking on an identity population the railway did not create and cannot fully observe. The mapping from contractor roles to railway permissions has to be defined, reviewed and versioned by the railway, and it has to be withdrawn when a contract ends, because the contractor's own account hygiene cannot do that work for us. The railway also becomes responsible for its own audit trail, since contractor sign-ins arrive as assertions and the meaning of those assertions has to be understood locally rather than assumed. What cannot be delegated is revocation. Because the trust runs one way, there is no facility for the railway to withdraw an identity at the contractor, so every mapping carries an expiry date and a review trigger rather than relying on a notification from the other side. What can be delegated is the contract itself, since the railway can require the contractor to run its own directory well, but only within the limits of what a one-way relationship makes visible.

questions.explanation: The railway owns the identity mapping, the audit trail and the revocation, because a one-way trust gives it no help from the other side. Contract terms can shape the contractor's hygiene but cannot carry the railway's duty.
questions.hint: Ask which duties the one-way link leaves with the railway.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a private endpoint does not do for authorisation
questions.learningObjective: Read the endpoint change correctly in the recorded activity

stimulus.body: At 22:15 the dispatcher recorded that the platform team had attached a private endpoint to the timetable data store for the depot display service. The engineer's note said the purpose was to keep depot traffic off the public network and recorded no change to the service's role. The next morning the store's log showed 1,904 reads from that service, all within the read actions its role allowed, and the security team noted that one of those reads had reached a table the service had never queried before.

questions.stem: On the evidence in the log above, which reading is correct?

options.text: The endpoint granted the service a wider reach, because a private path bypasses the role's limits
options.misconception: attributes extra authority to network placement

options.text: The new read is evidence of an error, because the endpoint should have blocked an unknown table
options.misconception: expects a private endpoint to filter by table

options.text: The endpoint explains the route, and the read follows from the role the service already holds
The new read is a compromise, because the service had no need of that table before the endpoint
options.misconception: treats any new behaviour as a compromise

questions.explanation: The note says the role did not change, so the read was permitted by an action the role already allowed. The endpoint changed where the traffic travelled, and neither it nor the log turns a permitted read into a compromise.
questions.hint: Ask what the engineer's note says about the role.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A signed link against a long-lived read key
questions.learningObjective: State why a signed link is safer and what must be true first
questions.stem: The depot service must fetch a feed, and today it uses a long-lived key. First state why a signed link is safer here, then state what must be true before the key is retired.

options.text: It is safer because it encrypts the feed, and the feed must publish a public key for the service
options.misconception: believes a signature encrypts the payload

options.text: It is safer because it cannot be replayed, and the feed must keep accepting the old key
options.misconception: believes a signed link can be replayed forever

options.text: It is safer because it hides the request, and the service must be given a private endpoint
options.misconception: confuses signing with network privacy

options.text: It is safer because it expires, and the feed must accept signed requests from the service

questions.explanation: Expiry is what bounds the value of a stolen link, so a signed request is the safer mechanism for a credential that will be copied at some point. The change only works when the feed can validate the service's signature, and the old key should be retired only once that is proven.
questions.hint: Ask what the feed has to validate.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Rewrapping and re-encrypting are different jobs
questions.learningObjective: Name the operation that changes only key material
questions.stem: A rotation over the manifest store changes only the key material around each ciphertext. Which statement describes that operation?

options.text: It rewraps the stored manifests, so the payload is never decrypted during the rotation
It re-encrypts the stored manifests, so the payload bytes change but the payload is protected
options.misconception: describes re-encryption but calls it key only

options.text: It re-signs the stored manifests, so the signature key is refreshed without re-encryption
options.misconception: confuses a signature key with an encryption key

options.text: It regenerates the stored manifests, so the contents are rebuilt from the source of truth
options.misconception: describes a rebuild rather than a key change

questions.explanation: Changing only the key material around an existing ciphertext is rewrapping, and the payload is never in the clear during the operation. Re-encryption would rewrite the stored bytes and expose the payload while it was being processed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the payload was ever in the clear.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Replacing a secret in a configuration file
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a rotation sequence that leaves the old value accepted
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log shows a configuration file edited at 02:00, a service restart at 03:10, and the old key still being accepted by the data store at 04:00. What does the sequence tell the reviewer?

options.text: The rotation succeeded, because the service was restarted after the file was edited
options.misconception: treats a restart as sufficient proof of rotation

options.text: The rotation is incomplete, because the old credential was still usable an hour later
The restart failed, because the service could not have started with the new value
options.misconception: infers a failed restart without evidence

options.text: The log is inconclusive, because the order of the entries proves nothing about the keys
options.misconception: dismisses a direct sequence of evidence

questions.explanation: Editing the file and restarting the service cover the first half of a rotation, but the old credential was still accepted an hour later. Until the old value is revoked the rotation is not complete, and the log records exactly that.
questions.hint: Ask when the old value stopped being accepted.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The blast radius of one identity provider
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the identities a set of federated systems brings in
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log records that 5 contractor systems federate into the railway's access system and that each brings 38 identities with it. How many federated identities can the railway expect to govern because of those five systems?
questions.explanation: Each of the 5 systems contributes 38 identities, and 5 times 38 gives 190 identities for the railway to govern. None of them arrives from a trust the railway controls at source, which is what makes the count matter.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of systems by the identities each brings.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A service principal and a platform identity are not the same
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the two credential types behave once leaked
questions.stem: The platform team is asked why a stored service principal should be replaced by a platform identity. Explain the difference in how the two behave when one leaks.

answer.exemplar: A stored principal leaks in ordinary ways: the value sits in a configuration file, it is pasted into a support ticket, it is copied into a test harness, or it is committed to a repository. Once copied it is a working secret for as long as the service presents it, and nothing about the credential expires, so the exposure is closed only if somebody notices and revokes it. A platform identity leaks in a much narrower way, because the platform issues it and holds no secret the application can leak, the application presents it through the platform's own mechanism rather than as a copied string, and the platform can expire it on a fixed schedule or disable it in seconds during an incident. The behavioural difference is therefore about time and about who can act: the platform identity has a bounded window and a central off switch, while the stored principal has neither and relies on hygiene in every place it is pasted.

questions.explanation: A copied stored principal stays usable until someone revokes it, while a platform identity can be expired centrally and quickly. The difference is the exposure window and who can close it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to each after a copy is made.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A permission boundary narrowing a role
questions.learningObjective: Count the roles a review actually narrowed

stimulus.body: The platform team reviewed 6 job roles. Three roles were narrowed by a permission boundary, one role was narrowed by a policy that denies particular actions, one role was unchanged, and one role carried both a boundary and a denying policy. The reviewer noted that the boundary on the fifth role was attached in production only and that the denying policy on the fourth role removed an action the role's definition allowed.

questions.stem: According to the role review above, which conclusion is sound?

options.text: Five roles are narrower, because the role with both controls should be counted twice
options.misconception: double counts the role carrying both controls

options.text: All six roles are narrower, because the review examined every role in the team
options.misconception: assumes being reviewed means being changed

options.text: Four roles are narrower, and the fifth differs between production and the test estate
Only the bounded roles are narrower, because a denying policy cannot restrict a role
options.misconception: believes a deny policy cannot remove an action

questions.explanation: Three bounded roles plus one role with a denying policy gives four narrowed roles, and the role with both controls counts once. The fifth role is bounded only in production, so the two environments now behave differently.
questions.hint: Ask which roles carry a control that removes actions.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Federation trust runs one way
questions.learningObjective: State what one-way federation gains and what it obliges
questions.stem: The signalling contractor federates one way into the railway's access system. First state what the railway gains from that arrangement, then state what it must accept.

options.text: The railway gains monitoring of contractor sessions, and it must accept the contractors' own leaver process
options.misconception: claims a visibility the one-way link does not provide

options.text: The railway gains the ability to issue tokens to contractor systems, and it must accept the extra sign-in path
options.misconception: reverses the direction of issued tokens

options.text: The railway gains nothing and accepts nothing, because a one-way link has no effect on either side
options.misconception: denies that a one-way link changes anything

options.text: The railway gains access for contractor engineers, and it must accept full responsibility for that access

questions.explanation: The contractor's provider being trusted means its engineers get into railway systems, which is the point of the arrangement. With no reverse trust the railway cannot push revocation out to the other side, so it keeps every governance duty for that access.
questions.hint: Ask who ends up responsible for the access.
